# Decode safe-handoff critical path and bounded optimization candidates — round 267

Status: read-only source/evidence review. No runtime work was performed. This report distinguishes committed measurements from source-based hypotheses. It does not qualify a performance change.

## Scope and pinned source

Reviewed WN source revision `0691bcdf5af63a85b3b25650f367d3276db64035` in `/home/yayoi/ghq/github.com/yqYo1/Strata/.worktree/sync-xe-v0143-nonfinite-20261012`. SHA-256:

- `src/program/generate.cpp`: `f9e6a45a4f7494cbc48c0b0e944b30d493f0ee97219fb2535a001f3a5913db05`
- `src/core/verify.cpp`: `efc5c8d37c1b6b18efa1a203c4ed8f0a4bc3c8c1098dbf0e87f8ab11cd845cad`
- `src/core/session.cpp`: `d914f75a19022edd29f6fec0fd4df85f1b24b09d56bf014744be79d12e914ab6`
- `src/core/expert_source.cpp`: `7915f5ceb462a5c14655bbe585408f72ef9abd581b95ed14f08d9533d20f2edc`
- `src/kernels/cpu/pool.cpp`: `c114539980d496ea69c17fee2ddaf1b7229668afe07586142f572d96cb8a7036`

The source’s own timing comments and counters are not external measurements. Source line references below refer to this pinned tree.

## What the committed measurements establish

Closed result `integrated-full32k-clean-results-v158.json` is registered as a clean, committed full-context comparison on the same source revision. It contains three 16-token runs per mode: overlap-off decode times 2094.7, 1768.2, and 1936.6 ms; overlap-on 2000.9, 2127.8, and 1985.0 ms. Those are 110.5–133.0 ms/output-token across this small sample, with substantial run-to-run variation. The result is performance eligible for comparison, not a qualification. It contains endpoint timings and matching-output evidence, but does not identify which host/queue interval dominates. These observations do not prove CPU pool work is the bottleneck.

The latest isolated pinned-thread CPU expert pair numbers relayed by Main (GU about 0.14–0.32 ms/expert; Down about 0.036–0.097 ms/expert) are microbenchmarks, not the pool’s per-layer critical path. Do not scale those numbers into a token estimate without the actual count, concurrency, cache behavior, and overlap. Neither those measurements nor the older R204/v0141 task-6 diagnostic attributes the current v0143 end-to-end latency. R204’s historical task-6 timings are not current-source evidence.

## Current path and boundaries

For the serial verifier path, `generate.cpp:9209–9230` takes the decode-start snapshot; each verifier window’s run, commit, and draft are separately timed (`9933–9941`), and the request endpoint is `decode_ms` at `9961`. `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING` reports average verify, GPU-reach wait, per-layer host service (with nested plan/activation-quantization/job-build/CPU-run values), stage, commit/emit, draft, and per-layer-window counts (`9967–9989`). This provides useful request/window decomposition, but its columns are not disjoint: the stage is nested in verify, per-layer host includes callbacks, and CPU/pool counters include phase scheduling/waits. Do not add all printed values as if they were independent wall intervals.

Inside `expert_pool_dispatch_multi`, `expert_source.cpp:1666–1672` begins a dispatch interval and calls `begin_layer`; the GPU resident/PCIe plan is built and published at `1673–1773` before the CPU work is dispatched, so copy-engine/GPU work can overlap the CPU pool. Input quantization for CPU misses, job construction, and pool dispatch follow in the same function; `d.ms_run` is host wall duration, not summed worker CPU cycles. The GPU hit callback records `hit_done`, and the Combine callback queries whether it was ready by the CPU-return boundary (`1981–1998`); `hit_ready` versus `hit_late` is an existing coarse overlap indicator. This is useful but does not attribute why a hit was late or how much time became exposed.

`ExpertPool::run_phase` (`pool.cpp:381–391`) waits for parked workers, publishes a phase, lets the host participate when enabled, waits for all tasks, and parks workers. Thus `ms_multi_gu`, `ms_multi_q`, and `ms_multi_down` around `run_phase` (`470–506`) measure host elapsed time including task scheduling and synchronization, not exclusive CPU busy time. The row chunks and phase counter timings should not be interpreted as worker-CPU execution alone.

The two handoff paths must be kept distinct:

- `session_loop` in `session.cpp:699–715` waits for a recorded GPU event before reading the mapped sequence/payload. It then launches resident GPU-hit work (`717–720`) while the host runs the CPU pool (`722–724`), copies misses and launches the combine/post graph, then enqueues the next pre graph (`733–780`). `gr.ms_to_ring` ends at the safe completed pre-graph handoff; `gr.ms_host` measures the host work/driver calls after observing the ring until the next pre graph is queued (`782–791`). `ms_to_ring` is a mixed interval (GPU pre work plus wait); `ms_host` is a useful exposed-driver/host interval, but includes CPU callback time and is not just driver overhead. The stream is finally synchronized (`793`).
- The serial verifier sets `segmented_` whenever the backend has not qualified concurrent host handoff (`verify.cpp:415–421`). A segmented graph ends at each host answer boundary (`1173–1183`). In `run`, the code waits for the completed segment before examining mapped sequence/payload, calls the CPU pool, drains copy work, raises the handshake flags, and then launches the next segment (`1514–1619`). This is the safe ownership policy. The spin/volatile route is used only if concurrent handoff is qualified (`1555–1567`). Preserve the completed-host boundary; do not make graph batching depend on volatile mapped reads or infer concurrency qualification from observed timing.

End-of-process `session_loop` summary has position denominators, explicitly because prefill also uses the loop (`generate.cpp:11251–11272`). Those cumulative `gr` counters cannot be treated as decode-only when prefill ran. Current request-scoped `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING` is better for the verifier path, but it does not expose the full `session_loop` subintervals or per-layer phase queue waits.

## Why 127 ms/token can persist beyond intrinsic math

The request’s decode time encloses verifier graph/queue execution, handoff waits, plan and fetch publication, activation conversion, job materialization, the CPU pool’s GU/Down phases and synchronization, combine/commit, and sampling/drafting. For `T=1`, each layer’s host boundary is serialized by the safe segmented path unless an independently qualified route is selected. Some GPU hit and asynchronous fetch work overlaps CPU service, so total CPU duration is not necessarily exposed duration. Conversely, graph submission/queue waits and a late GPU hit can extend the serial path even if individual expert kernels are fast. Existing counters give coarse clues (`verify` nested decomposition, `hit_ready/late`, and session-loop `ms_to_ring/ms_host`) but no complete per-layer causal timeline joined across CPU callback and GPU/copy queue completion. The 110–133 ms/token endpoint range therefore cannot be assigned to CPU math from current evidence.

## Two concrete optimization candidates (hypotheses only)

1. **Reduce host graph submissions in the safe `session_loop` route.** Prototype a captured continuation that combines `post[l]` and `pre[l+1]` into one graph launch after the current ring has completed and after the CPU pool/copy/combine callback has finished. Both existing graphs are already ordered on the same stream; current code launches them separately at `session.cpp:742` and `772`, with their intervening stream-ordered copy/combine. Keep exactly one completed event boundary before reading each ring; retain the existing final drain and error handling. This can only reduce host driver submissions / exposed post-ring latency; it does not reduce expert math. First verify that graph capture can include the copy/combine nodes and that all graph parameters/buffer lifetimes remain valid across replays. Benchmark only when `session_loop` is selected, with overlap on/off matched requests, using `ms_host` per layer and decode endpoint; record `ms_to_ring`, output parity, and queue completion errors. If `ms_host` is already small relative to endpoint time, this candidate has little headroom.

2. **Tune the existing CPU-versus-PCIe expert split using exposed service, not nominal CPU time.** `pcie_split_m` chooses the PCIe share before the CPU pool (`expert_source.cpp:1701–1705`); GPU copy launch and CPU pool run concurrently (`1724–1773`). A bounded tuning arm can change the split for one matched workload only after collecting per-layer distinct experts, RAM/cache hits, eligible pinned blobs, PCIe fetch enqueue/complete, CPU callback return, and GPU-hit ready/late-at-Combine. Move one expert at a time from the CPU share to PCIe (or vice versa) only when a layer’s *exposed* completion path is identified; avoid changing the ownership/flag protocol. Compare request decode latency and exact output IDs/logits while keeping cache, pool size, and request fixed. This may shorten the critical path if it balances the slower of CPU service and copy/GPU completion; it can also regress when PCIe completion becomes exposed. No split value is recommended from current data.

## Minimum bounded diagnostic before either optimization

One diagnostic request should emit a fixed-size, request-local aggregate per verifier window and layer (no per-expert timeline): route selected (`session_loop`/segmented verifier), `T`, distinct experts, CPU entries, resident hits, eligible and launched PCIe fetches; monotonic timestamps for segment/graph enqueue and completion, CPU callback enter/return, pool GU/activation-quantization/Down phase enter/return, copy-queue completion, hit event readiness at Combine, and next graph/segment enqueue. Include error/timeout state and an explicit ownership marker that mapped payload was read only after completed event/segment. Preserve intervals as overlapping events and compute exposed critical-path intervals from dependencies; do not sum nested timings. Keep this diagnostic separate from clean matched endpoint runs because detailed timestamps may perturb the result. First use one diagnostic request to rank candidate windows; then use repeated no-instrumentation clean endpoint comparisons and output parity to evaluate one optimization at a time.

This is the smallest evidence needed to tell whether a window’s tail comes from (a) host after-ring submission/synchronization, (b) CPU pool completion, (c) PCIe copy/fetch completion, or (d) GPU hit completion. If existing bounded counters already make a particular component clear, avoid adding redundant trace detail.

## Limits

No claim here demonstrates that either candidate improves the current model/device. No current active Main receipt or live process log was inspected. No source was changed and no build, test, GPU run, profiler run, or Git operation was performed. The shared source pointers are pinned to the stated WN revision; the closed v158 result and reported latest microbench are separate evidence classes and are not combined into a new timing estimate.
